result.title: A six-month periodic fasting reduces microalbuminuria and improves metabolic control in patients with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy: a randomized controlled study

knowledge_units.context_summary: A randomized controlled study compared a fasting-mimicking diet to a Mediterranean diet in patients with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy. The fasting-mimicking diet reduced microalbuminuria and improved metabolic markers like HOMA-IR and suPAR in the short term. The study suggests that the lack of changes in the detoxification of dicarbonyl compounds and markers for DNA damage may explain the recurrence of albuminuria at follow-up.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study investigates whether a six-month periodic fasting-mimicking diet reduces albumin-to-creatinine ratio in type 2 diabetes patients with diabetic kidney disease. It aims to link ACR reduction to changes in dicarbonyl detoxification, fatty acid oxidation, DNA damage, and senescence markers. The randomized, controlled, open study was conducted at the University Hospital in Heidelberg and involved patients with well-controlled diabetes and high ACR (American College of Rheumatology) scores.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study utilized stratified randomization based on BMI and HbA1c to assign participants to either a Fasting-Mimicking Diet or a Mediterranean Diet. The FMD was a plant-based diet with specific macronutrient compositions for different days, while the M-Diet maintained caloric intake and was adapted using the Mediterranean Diet Score. Participants on insulin therapy discontinued short-acting insulin and reduced long-acting insulin by 50% during FMD, with glycemic and blood pressure control monitored to maintain comparability between groups.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study defined the primary endpoint as the absolute difference in change of albumin-to-creatinine ratio between the fasting-mimicking diet and Mediterranean diet groups after six cycles. Secondary endpoints included changes in metabolic markers, dicarbonyl detoxification products, and DNA damage markers. The study utilized an intention-to-treat analysis with ANCOVA adjusted for baseline characteristics, and a sample size of 40 was calculated to detect a 30% reduction in ACR.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study found that a six-month periodic fasting-mimicking diet significantly reduced microalbuminuria and improved metabolic control in type 2 diabetes patients with diabetic nephropathy. The fasting-mimicking diet resulted in a 17% reduction in HbA1c and a 60% decrease in HOMA-IR in non-insulin-treated participants. The study found that the main reason for participants withdrawing was related to restrictions imposed as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The FMD group experienced greater weight loss than the M-Diet group, though body composition remained unchanged between groups. Plasma MG-H1 levels decreased significantly in the FMD group after three cycles, but this change did not correlate with ACR reduction. Participants who showed a reduction in ACR (Area Under the Curve) in the group with FMD (Fat-induced Modalkrankheit) had higher initial ACR values compared to those who did not respond to the treatment. Only the reduction in HOMA-IR (Homeostatic Model Assessment for Insulin Resistance) was maintained in the subsequent investigation.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study found that the diet, which was similar to fasting, was safe and well-tolerated, with most participants reporting no negative side effects. It led to a reduction in the use of medications to lower blood sugar and blood pressure in the group that followed the fasting-like diet, compared to the group that followed a Mediterranean diet. The FMD also caused a transient increase in blood ketones and a distinct response in fatty acid oxidation markers among ACR responders.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study found that the fasting-mimicking diet (FMD) only reduced microalbuminuria in patients with type 2 diabetes and diabetic nephropathy, with effects reversing after refeeding. The reduction in microalbuminuria was comparable to that seen with SGLT-2 inhibitors, but FMD did not affect macroalbuminuria, suggesting a point of no return after established renal damage. The diet led to reduced medication use and improved metabolic control, which was attributed to the diet itself, though independent pathways may be involved.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study found that the lack of change in methylglyoxal detoxification pathways and DNA repair during fasting-mimicking diet cycles correlates with the rapid increase in albuminuria after refeeding. The authors suggest that a sustained metabolic redirection, rather than just caloric restriction, is responsible for the observed changes. The study highlights the complexity of fasting interventions in type 2 diabetes, noting that while the control group was isocaloric, the FMD group experienced greater weight loss, which was statistically adjusted for.

knowledge_units.context_summary: The study concludes that the fasting-mimicking diet can reduce albuminuria and improve metabolic control in type 2 diabetes patients with microalbuminuria when combined with intensive diabetes care. The authors suggest that the lack of change in dicarbonyl detoxification and DNA-damage markers may cause albuminuria to relapse after six cycles, necessitating longer fasting periods. Future research should use larger cohorts and investigate renal cell metabolism, as the current study lacked kidney biopsies.
